title: Stream Falloff + History-Degradation Runthrough (Edge Cases)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked BlueOrbit through an edge-cases demo focusing on how long conversation history and high TPS affect streaming performance. Demonstrated console knobs, Optimize recommendations (batching/quantization), and a mitigation runbook for backpressure and timeouts. Customer requested specific benchmark spreadsheet and pilot steps; security questions on logs and KMS were raised.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-08-03 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Janelle Wu (Redwood), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (BlueOrbit), David Kim (BlueOrbit ML), Ella Sanchez (BlueOrbit Security)

Summary (auto): Edge-case demo showing how long context + high TPS interacts with streaming and KV cache. Showed console guardrails and Optimize suggestions.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Janelle): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick agenda — show the console, then live playbook for backpressure and a short Optimize run, then Q&A.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Carlos): hey, hi, real quick context — BlueOrbit mentioned replayer loads where they keep 20k token histories and have burst windows of 3k TPS for search reranking. we'll try to reproduce and show failure modes.
00:36 Priya: yep that's the pattern. most traffic is p95 spikes around 30 seconds, sustained for 2 minutes. we also have a long tail of chat sessions with 10–30k tokens.
00:50 Carlos: okay, cool. first thing — long context becomes KV-cache pressure. we saw eviction churn when prefix cache grows beyond memory and the runtime starts to stream from disk, which increases latency and causes backpressure in streaming paths.
01:12 David: couple clarifying q's — when you say eviction churn, does the runtime drop the entire session KV or partial? we saw weird partial responses.
01:25 Carlos: good question. typically we evict by LRU page granularity, but depending on configured cache TTL and the memory pressure threshold it can purge older KV entries which results in more attention recompute and sometimes repeated tokens or partial outputs in the stream because the model misses cached key-values mid-generation, so you'll see token jitter. sometimes transcription shows it as repeated words or sentence restarts.
01:50 Ella: from security, we want to ensure cache eviction doesn't leak other tenants — obviously dedicated pools are isolated but curious about logs and redaction.
02:03 Janelle: we'll include the KMS + audit log section in the security pack. quick demo — switching to the console.
02:15 [screen share noise]
02:22 Carlos: on the Console under "Routes" we set per-route max concurrency and preferred model variants. we're going to push a synthetic workload: 5k concurrent sessions, each with 12k token history and 1k TPS sustained per shard — this will stress KV and streaming. note: for hosted plans we have fallback policies to smaller quantized variants if latency SLOs breach.
02:47 Priya: we care more about correctness in some flows, so fallback to quantized models is OK only if we can compare top-k rerank results.
02:57 Carlos: understood. we'll show a canary that routes non-critical traffic to a 4-bit quantized variant while keeping critical traffic pinned to full fp16.
03:08 [demo noise: console toggles]
03:16 Carlos: starting the synthetic — watch the streaming panel, you'll see the active sessions and in-flight token graphs.
03:27 [synthetic load ramp noise — many coughs & keyboard]
03:34 Speaker 3 (Priya): already seeing latency creep — some streams are pausing then resuming.
03:40 Carlos: that's backpressure — the runtime's continuous batching queue backs up because per-token compute spiked due to cache misses and recompute. we have two mitigations: small-term (runtime level) — shed or throttle streaming frames, increase per-request timeout and enable prefix caching; longer-term — pre-warm KV for heavy sessions or tune compilation kernels for long sequences.
04:05 David: can you explain "shed streaming frames" — does that drop tokens?
04:11 Carlos: shed means we pause sending intermediate chunks to the client (so the model keeps computing) or we compress the streaming frames by merging them — you shouldn't lose final output but you'll see reduced granularity in partial results. only if queue overflow hits a hard limit will we drop sessions; that is a last-resort and controlled by the route policy.
04:33 Priya: hmm the partial results variance is a UX risk — for us we show incremental suggestions as the stream arrives. if granularity drops to a single final chunk it may feel slow.
04:44 Carlos: yes, tradeoff there. Optimize suggests adaptive chunking: increase chunk size during heavy compute to reduce per-chunk overhead and then decode bigger frames on client. we can also enable client-side heuristics to buffer until final chunk for certain routes.
05:02 Janelle: quick sidebar — Optimize just ran and suggested batching window adjustments and a quantization profile for the 30k context model that keeps p95 latency under your SLO at 60% of the original cost.
05:18 David: show the Optimize output.
05:21 [console: Optimize panel]
05:23 Carlos: here — it suggests two policies: 1) increase continuous batch max size to 64 for this workload; 2) set a KV-cache prewarm TTL of 10m for sessions flagged as heavy. also a recommendation to apply mixed-precision + 4-bit activation quant for non-critical routes.
05:42 Priya: the prewarm TTL, would that increase memory cost a lot?
05:47 Carlos: yes moderate increase — it's a tradeoff: higher memory footprint but fewer cache misses and less recompute, which lowers token cost and latency. Optimize provides estimated unit costs for both configurations — we'll share the sheet.
06:00 [30s silence, typing]
06:12 David: we need to understand observable signals — what dashboards should we watch to catch backpressure early?
06:18 Carlos: the Console has three charts to watch: queue depth, token compute per second, and streaming frame latency. set alerts on queue depth > 70% of concurrency threshold and token compute spikes above baseline by 2x. also instrument per-route dropped-frames metric.
06:36 Priya: ok. what about retries — our infra likes automatic client retries which may amplify spikes. any recommended retry strategy?
06:45 Carlos: yes, do exponential backoff with jitter, cap total retry attempts, and better: implement idempotency keys for non-chat endpoints so retries don't cause duplicate side effects. for streaming, prefer client-side buffering + resume tokens rather than blind retries.
07:03 Ella: on logs — we need audited request logs but redacted content. can we get token-level timing without payloads?
07:12 Janelle: yes, we provide timing traces and token counts but not raw user content in audit logs unless requested under enterprise contract; KMS integration for encrypted payloads is supported on Private.
07:26 [demo continues]
07:32 Carlos: watch here — after 7 minutes of high TPS the queue hit a soft limit, streaming frames started to be compressed and p95 latency jumped. then our routing policy triggered fallback for non-critical routes to a quantized variant. see how the active sessions for the critical route stayed pinned and maintained lower latency.
07:56 Priya: I see a few sessions ended with partial responses and an event in the console marked "stream-shedding: resumed with compressed payload" — those are the ones that might need client-side work.
08:07 Carlos: exactly. we have a backpressure runbook we follow: 1) identify affected routes via queue depth; 2) enable compressed streaming frames and raise chunk size; 3) if still above SLO, route non-critical traffic to quantized variants; 4) if capacity still scarce, autoscale dedicated pool or spin up cross-region fallback. the runbook is in the doc we'll share.
08:34 Priya: can you run through the expected cost delta for the different steps? like enabling prewarm vs routing to quantized models.
08:42 Carlos: rough numbers — prewarm increases baseline memory cost by ~12–20% but lowers token recompute cost by ~30% in our synthetic. quantized routing reduces per-token compute cost by ~45% but can degrade top-k ranking quality slightly; Optimize produces a table with estimated tokens-per-dollar for each config.
09:05 David: real question — how do we repro the partial repeated tokens issue? that's what bites our log parsers.
09:12 Carlos: it's usually caused by mid-generation KV misses that force attention recompute and triggers retransmit of previously generated tokens when the model reconciles sequence state. on the runtime level we added sequence-stable generation where the token buffer is reconciled before streaming out, but under extreme memory pressure you can get duplicates. we recommend a TTL-based eviction and prewarm as the primary fix.
09:40 Priya: would dedicated capacity eliminate this for us?
09:43 Carlos: Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor problems and gives you more predictable memory headroom. with Dedicated you can set a higher KV cache size and tighter eviction thresholds. but it's not a silver bullet: very large histories still require prewarm and sometimes model-level gradient adjustments (compilation kernels) for long sequences.
10:00 Priya: what about splitting history — can we compress or summarize old turns? we have some ideas to keep active KV smaller.
10:08 Carlos: yes, prefix summarization is a common pattern: maintain a condensed semantic summary for older turns and only keep the last N turns verbatim. that reduces KV footprint and preserves context. Optimize can help pick an optimal summarization frequency based on your QPS and token distribution.
10:25 David: let's talk timeouts — our frontend sets 30s request timeouts. is that too aggressive for long contexts?
10:31 Carlos: for generation that includes long context and heavy recompute, 30s can be too tight. in demo we saw p95 slip to 38s under heavy load. increment timeouts for those routes (60–90s) or use streaming with resumable tokens to avoid client timeouts. also, set conservative HTTP keepalive so connections aren't dropped prematurely.
10:50 Priya: about resumable tokens — how does that map to privacy? if we persist resume keys do they contain PII?
10:56 Carlos: resume tokens are opaque server-side handles; they map to a session pointer, not raw content. in Private you control where resume pointers persist. we'll document retention and redaction policies.
11:10 [brief silence]
11:16 Ella: security question: audit logs — can we get a per-token latency histogram without payloads, and can we route logs to our SIEM?
11:24 Janelle: yes to both. we support log forwarding (syslog/CloudWatch/BigQuery) with payload redaction, and the latency histograms are part of the trace export. we'll include the config snippets in the security pack.
11:40 Carlos: switching gears — quick technical deep-dive on compilation: long sequences often hit different kernel paths. we can compile an alternative kernel optimized for 32k contexts which reduces recompute overhead ~15% but increases memory usage; this is something our research team can build for you if you commit to a pilot.
12:05 Priya: how long to get that custom kernel?
12:08 Carlos: 4–6 weeks typical for a well-scoped model and sequence profile. that's in our enterprise roadmap.
12:15 David: can we see logs from today's synthetic run? specifically token compute per second and per-session drop events?
12:22 Carlos: yes, I'll attach a filtered log export after the call. those logs include approximate timestamps and event types; content redacted.
12:32 [typing]
12:40 Janelle: recapping next steps — we'll send the perf template and cost model, the security pack, and the runbook. Carlos will run the staging KV prewarm test and share results. BlueOrbit to provide QPS profiles. Then we schedule a pilot kickoff.
12:58 Priya: sounds good, thanks.
13:06 David: one last thing — our infra team is worried about auto-scaling lag. do you have playbacks for cross-region failover?
13:12 Carlos: yes, we demoed cross-region fallback briefly — the runtime can reroute routes by policy with a brief cold-start for model weights; we can set warm standby pools for critical routes which cost more but reduce cold-start. we'll include estimated cold-start time in the doc.
13:28 Ella: appreciate the security details.
13:32 Janelle: thanks all — we'll follow up.
13:37 [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription: filler words, occasional wrong labeling of speakers, some technical acronyms mis-transcribed (e.g., "K V cash"), and punctuation may be off.

References mentioned: perf-template.xlsx (link to be sent), security-pack.zip (SOC2 + KMS integration), runbook-backpressure.md (Redwood internal runbook excerpt to share), optimize-recommendations.csv
